name: Shang Dynasty
capital: Yin (near Anyang); earlier Bo, Ao and others
summary: The earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by written records, known for bronze vessels and oracle-bone inscriptions, China’s earliest writing.

knownFor.label: Oracle bones
knownFor.note: The earliest Chinese writing, carved on bones for divination.

knownFor.label: Ritual bronzes
knownFor.note: Large cast bronze vessels for ancestor rites.

knownFor.label: Chariots
knownFor.note: Horse-drawn chariots appear in late Shang tombs.

location.value: The middle and lower Yellow River valley, centred on modern Henan. The last capital, Yin, was near modern Anyang.

terrain.value: Loess plains and the Yellow River floodplain, with the Taihang Mountains to the west. Millet was farmed in the north and rice along the Yangtze.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Shang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

climate.value: Probably warmer and wetter than today. Oracle bones record elephant and rhinoceros hunts in the north China plain.
climate.source: Elvin, The Retreat of the Elephants (2004)

resources.value: Fertile loess soils for millet. Copper, tin and lead for bronze were brought from distant sources.

disasters.value: Oracle-bone divinations constantly ask about rain, drought, harvests and floods. The specific disasters are not documented.

population.value: No reliable estimate exists for the Shang population.

urbanisation.value: Large walled centres. The Zhengzhou Shang City walls ran about 7 km around (15th century BCE). The Yanshi city covered nearly 200 hectares, Huanbei about 470 hectares, and the late capital Yinxu was larger still.

disease.value: Illness appears only in oracle-bone divinations, for example questions about the king’s toothache. There are no records of epidemics.

migration.value: According to tradition, the capital moved five times before the king Pan Geng settled it at Yin.

economicBase.value: Agriculture (millet) supplemented by hunting and animal husbandry. Bronze production was on a large scale by about 1500 BCE.

tradeRoutes.value: Cowrie shells found at Anyang show contact with coastal peoples. Metals and jade came from distant regions. Sea trade was very limited.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible. Wealth was concentrated in royal and aristocratic tombs.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells were used as valuables and money ("shell money"). The king received tribute from royal estates and allied rulers.

inequality.value: Extreme. Royal tombs held hundreds of bronzes and human sacrifices, while commoners were conscripted for labour and war.

governmentType.value: A monarchy. The king led ancestor worship and divination, and royal kin held estates and paid tribute.

keyRulers.value: Tang (founder, c. 1600 BCE). Pan Geng (moved the capital to Yin). Wu Ding (c. 1250–1191 BCE). Fu Hao (Wu Ding’s consort and a military general). Di Xin (last king, c. 1075–1046 BCE).

succession.value: Hereditary within the royal Zi clan. In earlier generations the throne often passed from brother to brother before passing to the next generation.

institutions.value: An early form of bureaucracy with titled officials (“Many Dog officers”, “Many Archers”, “Many Artisans”). Scribes kept divination records and counts of enemies killed, prisoners and booty.

stability.value: Capital moves suggest periods of instability, but internal revolts are poorly documented.

eliteConflict.value: Later Zhou texts blame the last king Di Xin’s cruelty and excess for the fall. These accounts were written by the Zhou, who overthrew him.

armyAndTech.value: The king kept about 1,000 troops at the capital. Border campaigns used 3,000–5,000 troops, and up to 13,000 against rebellions. Weapons included bronze spears and dagger-axes and composite bows. Chariots appeared around 1200 BCE.

majorWars.value: Long wars against northern and western peoples such as the Guifang and the Qiang. Defeat by the Zhou at the Battle of Muye, c. 1046 BCE.

territoryChange.value: Wikipedia’s infobox gives an approximate extent of about 1,250,000 km² around 1122 BCE. Shang influence reached the Yangtze (Panlongcheng).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included the Guifang and the Qiang, many of whom became sacrificial captives. The Zhou were first a western ally or vassal, then the conqueror.

inventions.value: Bronze casting on a large scale (ritual vessels, weapons) and oracle-bone inscriptions, the earliest Chinese writing.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Shang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

scienceEducation.value: Oracle bones record observations of eclipses, Mars and comets, and a lunisolar calendar. Literacy was limited to scribes and diviners.

openness.value: Adopted the horse-drawn chariot, probably from the northern steppes, around 1200 BCE.

communicationTransport.value: Chariots, which first appeared about 1200 BCE.

religion.value: Divination and sacrifice to royal ancestors, nature spirits and the high god Di. State rituals included animal and human sacrifice.

languageWriting.value: Oracle-bone script, the ancestor of Chinese characters. The oldest surviving inscriptions date to about 1250 BCE. More than 20,000 oracle bones were excavated in the 1920s–30s, and over four times as many have been found since.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Shang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

artsArchitecture.value: Ritual bronze vessels (ding, gu) decorated with taotie masks, and jade carving. The tomb of Fu Hao (excavated 1976) contained over 200 bronze ritual vessels. Palaces were built on rammed-earth platforms at Yinxu.

socialStructure.value: The royal family, aristocrats, and town and rural commoners who were conscripted for labour and war. Most sacrificial victims were war captives. Some people buried with royals may have been slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Held together by the royal ancestor cult and the ritual authority of the king. The name “Yin” for the dynasty seems to come from the later Zhou.

dailyLife.value: Commoners lived in pit houses; nobles in rammed-earth halls. Millet, wheat and rice; bronze vessels for feasts.

neighbours.value: The Guifang, the Qiang and the Zhou to the north and west. Distinct bronze-age cultures such as Sanxingdui in Sichuan.

ideasReligions.value: After the conquest, Shang descendants ruled the state of Song, which kept Shang rites until Qi conquered it in 286 BCE.

colonisation.value: Expanded through allied and outpost settlements, for example Panlongcheng on the Yangtze.

riseSignals.value: Tradition says Tang overthrew Jie, the last ruler of the Xia (Xia’s historical existence is debated). Control of bronze production, walled cities and ritual authority underpinned Shang power.

peakPeriod.value: After the capital moved to Yin under Pan Geng, especially the reign of Wu Ding (c. 1250–1191 BCE).

declineSignals.value: Later sources describe misrule under Di Xin and draining wars with neighbours. These accounts come from the Zhou victors.

outcome.value: Conquered by the Zhou at the Battle of Muye, c. 1046 BCE. Di Xin is said to have killed himself. The Zhou justified the conquest with the Mandate of Heaven.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Shang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Zhou dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Oracle bones and archaeology (Yinxu, Zhengzhou, Yanshi), plus much later texts (the Shiji, and the Bamboo Annals, whose surviving manuscripts are of disputed authenticity). Dates and figures were checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Keightley (1978) and Li Feng (2013).

overallCertainty.value: Low to moderate. Traditional dates (c. 1600–1046 BCE) are approximate, and at least 44 end dates between 1130 and 1018 BCE have been proposed. Written evidence only begins around 1250 BCE.
